extracted.intended_audience: general readers, artists, critics, and students of aesthetics and literature
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes Tolstoy's criteria for what counts as art, what makes art good or bad, and how to judge artistic works (focus on transmission of feeling, sincerity, subject-matter, accessibility, and moral aim). Useful for writers, critics, and students of creative writing and aesthetics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of art — transmission of feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: “Art is a human activity... The object of this activity is to transmit to others feeling the artist has experienced.” Art is a means of union among men, joining them together in the same feelings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art’s core purpose is emotional transmission: through external signs (movements, lines, colours, sounds, arrangements of words) an artist 'infects' others so they share his feelings. Evaluate works by whether they actually communicate the artist’s feeling to an audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test of art — infection (internal test)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The test of art is infection.” If an author has moved you so that you feel as he felt, the work that has so infected you is a work of art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge art primarily by an internal/empathic test: does the work make you experience the same feeling the artist intended? Note the requirement of successful transmission — mere intention is insufficient without actual infection. Distinguish genuine infection from mere physiological reactions or clever technical effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate expression / clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: “Without adequate expression there is no art, for there is no infection, no transference to others of the author’s feeling.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A work must find a clear, effective mode of expression to transmit feeling. Evaluate the clarity and appropriateness of the chosen medium and formal devices (words, sounds, colors, lines, movements) in producing emotional contagion. Poor or obscure expression negates artistic effect even if the feeling exists in the artist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intentionality of transmission
rubrics_metrics.description: “Art begins when some one, with the object of making others share his feeling, expresses his feeling by certain external indications.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A critical requirement is that the expression be purposeful — not accidental or purely reflexive (e.g., yawning that causes others to yawn). Distinguish incidental influence from deliberate art: only the latter counts as art under Tolstoy’s definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity of feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: “The one great quality which makes a work of art truly contagious is its sincerity.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The feelings expressed must be genuinely those of the author (not borrowed for effect, money, fame, or fashion). Sincerity compels the artist to seek clear expression and tends to produce originality. Anti-patterns: art produced for commercial gain, prestige, or imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality rooted in authentic feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: “The man who is not borrowing his feelings, but has drawn what he expresses from the depths of his nature, is sure to be original.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originality is judged by authenticity of emotional source rather than novelty for its own sake. Work that genuinely springs from the artist’s inner experience is likelier to offer a distinctive, convincing expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universality / accessibility to common people
rubrics_metrics.description: True art is infectious to normal human beings, including the 'country peasant of unperverted taste'; it 'infects any man whatever his plane of development.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a work can unite broad audiences (across class, education, generation) in the same feeling. Anti-patterns: art that only pleases a narrow cultured elite or requires specialized 'recognised authorities' to validate it. Examples: folk-songs, Gospel parables, Burns, Bunyan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of artistic perfection — degree of universality
rubrics_metrics.description: A work of art that united every one with the author, and with one another, would be perfect art; the nearer a work approaches universal infection, the nearer it approaches perfection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing works, consider how widely and durably they unite people in common feeling (across generations, races, social strata). Greater universality counts as higher artistic achievement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject-matter criterion — moral/social value (religious perception)
rubrics_metrics.description: The best art transmits feelings 'flowing from the highest perception... of our right relation to our neighbour and to the Source from which we come.' Tolstoy identifies the 'religious perception' of his time as the consciousness that well-being lies in the growth of brotherhood among men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge subject-matter by whether the feelings spread by the work conduce to human well‑being and brotherhood. Use an ethical/religious-perception standard to decide whether transmitted feelings are beneficial or harmful. Anti-patterns: art that promotes violence, sectarianism, selfish patriotism, or other feelings that harm collective well‑being.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible subject-matter types
rubrics_metrics.description: Tolstoy: the subject-matter of best art can be of two kinds — (1) feelings from the highest perception attainable (promoting brotherhood), and (2) simple feelings of common life, accessible to everyone, provided they do not hinder progress toward well‑being.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept both lofty, morally formative themes and sincere, simple common‑life feelings so long as they are harmless or constructive. Examples: Dickens’ 'Christmas Carol' (compassion), nursery rhymes, folk-stories. Reject works spreading harmful sentiments even if technically accomplished.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish art from mere popularity or critical opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Popularity among the masses or approval by critics does not alone establish artistic value; critics, publishers, and the public often cannot tell true art from counterfeits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid equating contemporary vogue or authoritative endorsement with artistic merit. Apply the internal test of infection and moral subject-matter rather than relying on critics' fashions or temporary popularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejecting physiological or purely intellectual effects as art
rubrics_metrics.description: Art is not merely something that produces a physiological effect (lulling or exciting) or an intellectual puzzle that gives people something to think about; such effects are often mistaken for art by the 'cultured crowd.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating, separate purely sensory/physiological thrills or cerebral cleverness from genuine emotional contagion rooted in sincere feeling. Works that only excite, soothe, or puzzle without transmitting shared feeling should not be considered true art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art versus science — different aims and evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: “Science investigates... Art transmits these truths from the region of perception to the region of emotion.” Science requires preparation; art can 'infect any man whatever his plane of development.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that art’s success is measured by emotional transmission rather than by argumentative clarity or evidence. However, art may incorporate scientific truths by making them felt. Do not evaluate artistic effectiveness solely by standards appropriate to scientific inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and avoidance of pseudo‑erudition
rubrics_metrics.description: Tolstoy condemns 'elaborate theories' and 'ponderous pseudo-erudition' that obscure the subject; he values compressing large subjects without being intolerably dry and insists readers be alert to follow him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer clear, direct expression that serves infection and accessibility. Beware of style that prioritizes learned display over sincere communication of feeling; such verbosity or abstruseness can block emotional transmission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social distribution and responsibility of art
rubrics_metrics.description: Tolstoy objects to art produced and endowed at great social cost when many labourers lack necessities (example: building an expensive Opera House while labourers suffer). He notes that often artists produce 'spiritual food' primarily for the cultured class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether artistic production and patronage are socially responsible and whether the works produced reach or serve the broader population. Consider equity of access and whether art fosters common human bonds rather than exclusive consumption by elites.
